newsitem.title: USA: Christmas tree mulch, the green way to go.
newsitem.headline: Christmas tree mulch, the green way to go.

text.p: The fresh scent of pine has faded, needles have dropped and 37 million Christmas trees are waiting to be dumped. For the revellers who agonized over chopping a live tree for the holidays, mulching is the path to redemption.

Green groups say composting a farm-grown tree instead of just discarding it is better than reusing a fake tree year after year. "Over the long run, I think that will provide us with a better solution -- sustainably growing a renewable resource, composting afterwards, returning nutrients to the soil," Jackie Prince Roberts of the Environmental Defence Fund said.
But the advantage of farm-grown trees is lost when they end up in garbage dumps, as most do.

The choice between real and artificial trees boils down to pesticides versus PVC (polyvinyl choloride). "That's a hard trade-off," Jay Feldman, executive director of the National Coalition Against the Misuse of Pesticides, said.

About 40 different fertilisers and pesticides that are recommended for Christmas tree plantations can contaminate groundwater and even leave toxic traces in homes, Feldman said. But that has not turned green advocates into fans of fake trees, because PVC is made of non-renewable petroleum-based chemicals, manufactured at plants that pollute the air.

About 25 to 30 million pounds of recycled PVC go into trees and garlands each year, about 10 pounds per seven-foot tree, according to the Vinyl Institute. The film used for trees is almost entirely made of PVC left over from the production of packaging material, keeping it out of landfills "for a long time," said Robert Burnett, executive director of the institute.
But plastic treemakers are slow to play up the environmental benefits of their trees.

"The environmental issue is probably far less significant than the safety issue," said Claus Beckroge, vice president of General Foam Plastics Corp., the largest U.S. producer of artificial trees. "When dried out, (live trees) are extreme fire hazards," he said. By contrast, PVC, which contains chlorine, can extinguish fires.

A tree-planting group, Global Releaf, said it advocated using fresh trees instead of fake, especially if the trees were replanted. "We don't really have a problem with trees from Christmas tree farms, as long as they're growing them on a sustainable basis and are conscientious with chemicals," spokesman Dan Smith said.
